newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish election overshadowed by rate rise/EMU fears.
newsitem.headline: Irish election overshadowed by rate rise/EMU fears.

text.p: Irish financial markets will be wary but not panicked by a minority government outcome to Ireland's general election, economists said on Sunday, noting that currency concerns and EMU continue to hold centre stage.

The centre-right opposition of Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrat alliance fell two seats short of a majority, holding 81 out of 166 seats, and will need the backing of Independents to control a majority in parliament.
The shape and make-up of the new government will not be known until parliament resumes on June 26 to elect a new Prime Minister, which is certain to be Ahern, analysts said.

Economists said a minority government would cause some uncertainty but market sentiment would be dominated by pressure on the Irish currency and concern that EMU, Europe's planned economic and monetary union, might be delayed.
"It was the least favoured outcome and will lead to a bit of uncertainty but the market reaction will be muted," AIB Capital Markets economist Pat O'Sullivan told Reuters.
He said the market was more concerned about the prospect of an interest rate rise by Ireland's central bank which is deemed on the cards if the Irish pound falls below 90 pence sterling.
"If sterling opens up around 2.80-2.83 marks and the Irish market under-performs, the stg/Irish cross might fall below 0.9000 stg and that would be likely to lead to a rate hike," he said.
By 1915 GMT on Sunday the Irish pound was quoted at 0.9120/50 stg and 2.5733/48 marks.

The Irish unit has taken a concerted battering over recent weeks as operators sold the currency on speculation that Ireland will enter EMU at its central European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) level of 2.41 marks.
Some economists said that the new government may reconsider the merits of a revaluation of the currency within the ERM grid as a means of tackling the currency dilemma.
"The market will be interested to see the incoming government's attitude to the falling punt," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin said.
"There is a school of thought that we should go for a revaluation. We could have five percent revaluation and move our central rate up to 2.55 marks instead of 2.41 marks."
McLaughlin said PD leader Harney would not have favoured such a move but her influence now was stunted by her poor performance in the polls.
Economists shrugged off recent comments by Ahern ruling out a revaluation of the currency as nothing more than pre-election lip service.

Fianna Fail's Charlie McCreevy is generally expected to get the post of Finance Minister within the new government, economists said, adding that such a move would meet with the approval of the market.

"I would say McCreevy will get the finance minister role and that will be welcomed by the market as he is expected to keep a tight rein on spending," Bank of Ireland Group Treasury economist Jim Power said.

The combative 47-year-old Kildare accountant will have the enviable task of presiding over an Irish economic boom, low inflation, abundant coffers and more room to manoeuvre than for the past decade or more.
He has been unwavering in his commitment, over the years, to cut government spending, reduce taxes and slash the national debt of 30 billion Irish pounds ($44.4 billion).

McCreevy said that if he is made finance minister government spending will not increase above the inflation rate plus 2.0 percent, a total spend of four percent against the current government's eight percent.
"You have to decide what spending will be and then stick to it," McCreevy told Reuters the day before the poll.
